# DnsResolver v1.0.0

The first stable release of **DnsResolver**, a C++23 library for parsing,
building, and resolving DNS messages against an in-memory authoritative
zone — a typed, RFC 1035-conformant packet representation with correct
compression-pointer handling, not a raw-bytes wrapper.

## Highlights

- **RFC 1035 wire-format packet structs** — `Header`, `Name`, `Question`,
  `ResourceRecord`, and `Message`, under `DnsPro::Packet`, giving parsed
  DNS messages a typed, structured representation rather than raw bytes.
- **`Parser`: bytes → `Message`** — offset-driven, single-pass parsing,
  with DNS name-compression pointer support (RFC 1035 §4.1.4) including
  rejection of forward/self-pointers and pointer loops
  (`Status::COMPRESSION_FORWARD_POINTER`, `Status::COMPRESSION_LOOP`).
- **Loop detection that catches oscillation, not just backward jumps** —
  a label that advances the cursor forward, followed by a pointer back
  to that label, still satisfies a naive "each hop must be backward"
  rule while looping forever. `Parser` bounds total hops with a step
  counter specifically to catch this class of malformed packet.
- **`Builder`: `Message` → bytes** — always writes full, uncompressed
  names. This is a deliberate simplification, not a correctness gap:
  round-trip correctness only requires that a rebuilt packet re-parse to
  an equivalent `Message`, not that it match another encoder's
  compression choices byte-for-byte — at a real, measured wire-size and
  build-time cost documented in Benchmarks rather than an unmeasured one.
- **`ZoneStore`** — an in-memory, case-insensitive (RFC 4343) authoritative
  record store, indexed `HashMap<string, HashMap<uint16_t, Vector<ResourceRecord>>>`
  (`name → type → records`) so `lookup()` and `removeRecord()` stay
  independent of zone size rather than degrading as the zone grows.
- **`Resolver`** — ties `Parser` + `ZoneStore` + `Builder` into a single
  `resolve()` call: raw query bytes in, raw response bytes out, with
  correct NOERROR/NXDOMAIN/NODATA handling.
- **Zero-copy `Message` moves** — move-construct and move-assign cost
  ~6 ns regardless of how many questions or answer records a `Message`
  holds, since `Vector`'s move steals the underlying buffer pointer
  rather than copying elements.
- Built directly on `VectorPro` and `HashMapPro`, vendored as git
  submodules under `libs/internal/` (`ArenaAllocator` is also vendored
  there but not yet wired into anything).

## Performance

The parse/build/lookup paths are designed around avoiding unnecessary
allocation, copying, and scanning:

- Nested `name → type → records` indexing in `ZoneStore` keeps
  `lookup()` and `removeRecord()` cost independent of zone size —
  measured flat at ~144 ns/op whether the zone holds 100 or 10,000
  names.
- `Message` move-construct/move-assign cost ~6 ns regardless of how
  many questions or answer records the message holds, since `Vector`'s
  move steals the underlying buffer pointer rather than copying
  elements.
- Compression-pointer following in `Parser::parseName()` adds real,
  bounded overhead over an uncompressed name — the one place
  decompression cost shows up directly in the numbers below.
- `Builder` skips compression entirely, trading wire size for a
  simpler, allocation-light encode path with no back-reference
  bookkeeping.

## Benchmarks

Solo-timed at 10K / 100K / 1M iterations — no reference implementation
exists to compare against (there's no standard-library or widely-used
DNS parser/zone-store to pair each benchmark with). Full dataset:
`benchmarks/baselines/v1.0.0.json`.

| Operation | DnsPro (1M) |
|---|---|
| `Parser::parse()` — query, single question | 62.97 ns/op |
| `Parser::parse()` — response, 4 answer records | 296.11 ns/op |
| `Builder::build()` — query, single question | 122.20 ns/op |
| `Builder::build()` — response, 4 answer records | 399.52 ns/op |
| `ZoneStore::lookup()` — existing name+type | 137.71 ns/op |
| `ZoneStore::lookup()` — missing name | 61.89 ns/op |
| `Resolver::resolve()` — answer found | 448.81 ns/op |
| `Resolver::resolve()` — NXDOMAIN | 360.46 ns/op |
| `Message` move-construct | 5.99 ns/op |
| Name parse — uncompressed | 63.46 ns/op |
| Name parse — via compression pointer | 96.05 ns/op |

A few things worth calling out honestly:

- **`Resolver::resolve()` is the most expensive path measured**
  (360–449 ns/op), unsurprising since it chains parse, zone lookup, and
  build together — but each individual stage stays under 400 ns/op, so
  the full pipeline doesn't add overhead beyond the sum of its parts.
- **A missing-name lookup is faster than a hit, not slower**
  (61.89 ns vs. 137.71 ns) — a miss short-circuits at the outer
  name-level hash lookup, while a hit has to additionally walk the
  inner `type → records` index to find and return the matching
  records.
- **Compression costs a real, bounded premium**: resolving a name
  through one pointer hop takes ~51% longer than an uncompressed name
  (96.05 ns vs. 63.46 ns) — the one place decompression's cost shows up
  directly rather than being amortized away.
- **`ZoneStore::lookup()` stays flat from 100 names up to 10,000**
  (~144 ns/op either way), confirming the nested hash index does its
  job — zone size stops being a cost variable in the lookup path.

## Testing

The project includes a comprehensive test suite covering:

- Unit-level correctness for `Parser`, `Builder`, `ZoneStore`, and the
  `Packet` structs in isolation
- Cross-component integration: full parse → build round trips and
  `Resolver::resolve()` against a populated `ZoneStore`
- Regression coverage pinning every bug fixed during development (loop
  detection, forward-pointer rejection, name-compression edge cases)
  so none of them can silently return
- Lifecycle scenarios spanning multi-question, multi-record messages
- Concurrency correctness — `ZoneStore` currently has no internal
  locking, so this suite deliberately exercises the real
  unsynchronized write race rather than asserting correctness

Both the project's own `custom/` framework and an equivalent
`google_tests/` suite cover the same categories, and both run together
via `ctest`.

## Code Coverage

The current test suite achieves:

- **89.2% line coverage** (265 / 297 lines)
- **86.2% function coverage** (25 / 29 functions)

Coverage reports exclude test infrastructure and submodule dependencies
(`libs/internal/`, GoogleTest/GoogleMock), focusing on DnsPro's own
implementation in `include/DnsPro/` and `src/DnsPro/`.

## Continuous Integration

Automated builds, tests, and checks are configured across:

- Multi-compiler, multi-OS builds (GCC + Clang on Ubuntu, MSVC on
  Windows, AppleClang on macOS, each Debug and Release)
- An ASan/UBSan job on Linux — there is no separate TSan job, since
  `ZoneStore` isn't internally synchronized yet
- `clang-format` and `clang-tidy` checks on every push and pull request
- Code coverage collection via `lcov`, with submodule and
  test-infrastructure sources excluded from the measured result
- CodeQL security analysis, on every push/PR to `main` plus a weekly
  scheduled scan
- Conan and vcpkg packaging, each verified with a real consumer smoke
  test against the built package

*(`clang-format` and `clang-tidy` currently run with
`continue-on-error` — informational, not yet merge-blocking — worth
tightening before relying on them as a hard gate.)*

## Release

This release represents the first stable version of DnsResolver and
establishes its complete core API surface: typed wire-format structs,
bidirectional parse/build with compression-pointer support, an
authoritative in-memory zone store, and a resolver tying them together
into a single raw-bytes-in, raw-bytes-out call.

## Installation

Clone the repository and integrate DnsResolver into your C++ project using
the provided CMake configuration.

See the project documentation for build instructions, API usage, and
integration details.
